title: Andy Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
description: Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.The prime minister and US p
body: Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship"."We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France Van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables."Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies. "The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

schema.headline: Andy Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting

title: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose
description: Figure caption, Watch: Presley Gerber seen alongside his family on the red carpetByChris Graham and Grace Eliza GoodwinOfficials are investigating the
body: Figure caption, Watch: Presley Gerber seen alongside his family on the red carpetByChris Graham and Grace Eliza GoodwinOfficials are investigating the death of Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, as a suspected overdose, Santa Monica police said on Monday. The 27-year-old model died at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. The exact cause of death has not been determined, police said, adding there was no indication of foul play.Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US partner CBS News: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Presley Gerber became a model like his mother and sisterHe went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.In recent years, Presley Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use. In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do." And in this month's American Vogue, external, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone."I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."She added: "My parents for most of our lives were very, very private and didn't share anything - and now we have this absolute teacher, my brother, who says, 'I'm gonna be very human for everyone.' There's only so much you can hide from the world. And trying to put a lid on something just makes the person feel like you're ashamed of them."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Gerber (left) was a model and had spoken about his close relationship with his familyGerber had previously spoken of his close relationship with his family, including Kaia, who he appeared alongside in a campaign for Calvin Klein in 2018, and whose name he had tattooed on his arm.He told People Magazine that year: "We're a close family, especially me and my sister, so it's definitely cool. "We get to travel together half of the time, so it makes it a lot less lonely."Gerber also starred alongside his mother in Pepsi's 2018 Super Bowl commercial, 26 years after Crawford first appeared in her famous 1992 advertisement for the brand."We're a really tight family, so it was just like going to work with one of your friends. It was so fun, and easy," he told People Magazine at the time.In July, Crawford shared two childhood photographs of her son on Instagram to mark his 27th birthday."I'm so proud of the man you've become, but I'll always see you as my little boy! Love you," she wrote.If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: Death of Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose

title: Andros Townsend: Being run over by pitch roller was 'terrifying'
description: Former England winger Andros Townsend has described the moment he was run over by a pitch roller in Thailand as "terrifying".The 35‑year‑old former To
body: Former England winger Andros Townsend has described the moment he was run over by a pitch roller in Thailand as "terrifying".The 35‑year‑old former Tottenham, Luton and Crystal Palace forward, now with PT Prachuap in Thai League 1, was warming up for a match in Pattani on Saturday when a member of staff appeared to lose control of a heavy pitch roller.Townsend's left leg briefly got stuck under the vehicle, but he was unhurt. He came off the bench late on in a 3-0 win.Speaking about the incident for the first time on Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored, Townsend said he was lucky to only escape from under the roller with a few "bumps and bruises"."Every time I see it, I'm cringing, I'm in disbelief," he said."It's horrible to watch back and to see what could have been, thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall onto the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me."Townsend, who won 13 caps for England, said that he did think it was strange to see two rollers either side of the pitch during the warm-up."I remember thinking to myself, 'I've never seen that before in my career, what are they doing?' But we got called to warm-up. Didn't think anything of it," he said."The next I saw him was when I was literally underneath him and thankfully no serious damage. A couple of bumps and bruises but managed to walk away unscathed, luckily."Townsend, who has had numerous setbacks with injuries during his career, said the roller incident was "definitley not going to stop me from continuing"."They (his team-mates) were very surprised that I continued the warm-up. They were telling me to go to the doctor," he said."It was quite heavy, but I was able to kind of lift [it], force it off me. So when it was completely on me, I was getting crushed a little bit."I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my team-mates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say."Townsend was concerned his ankle and left knee, which have both been operated on, would be damaged in the incident.He said: "I thought, either my left ankle was going to snap or my left knee is going to snap. I thought I was done. I was very fortunate that I was able to hobble away and recover within a few minutes."The midfielder made light of the incident on Instagram, referencing one of his recent posts in which he compared a sun-drenched Thai away trip with previous visits to Stoke's Bet365 Stadium.He wrote: "It turns out Stoke away wasn't so bad after all."

schema.headline: Andros Townsend: Being run over by pitch roller was 'terrifying'

title: Schools 'crying out' for guidance from government on AI, report warns
description: Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned.Sir Anthon
body: Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned.Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic".His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year.The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation.Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival.Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely.His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine.The report recommends a 10-point plan for AI in education in England, including:The prime minister delivering a landmark speech to set out the importance of aligning education with how AI is used in the real worldSchools and colleges developing their own AI strategies, and having Ofsted assess their implementation as part of its inspectionsA mass information campaign to set out the opportunities and risks of AIUsing AI to transform the way schools and colleges collect and use data to track pupil progressReforming assessments into a "two-lane" system of both exams and a "continuous evaluation of a student's understanding" using AIThe report says its poll of young people suggests many of those who responded thought AI was making education less important in their lives, with some saying it could eventually replace teachers and make universities "useless"."Put simply, education has not kept pace with how – and how much – young people are already using AI, and that gap is starting to show up as a loss of perceived value in the institution itself," the report says.A spokesperson for the Department for Education says ministers take the "significant opportunities and challenges" of AI "incredibly seriously".As well as refreshing the curriculum in England, they say they are building new AI tutoring tools and introducing new vocational routes to get children into successful careers.Some schools have already embedded AI into the curriculum. Benjamin Barker, principal at King's Leadership Academy in Liverpool, says he wants his students to learn how to use tools safely, while also developing their critical thinking skills.Student Emma, 12, says she uses AI for her robotics projects, as well as proof-reading her English homework, and believes more students should be taught how to use it responsibly."AI is coming into the future. It's getting more advanced," she says."There's no way we're going to completely pull back from it. So I think that we should use it to be better people."

schema.headline: Schools 'crying out' for guidance from government on AI, report warns

title: Arrests as migrant boat reaches Folkestone without being intercepted
description: Five people have been detained and sent to border security command after a migrant boat reached Kent without being intercepted.The dinghy made it to s
body: Five people have been detained and sent to border security command after a migrant boat reached Kent without being intercepted.The dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone on Monday morning. The Home Office says an investigation has begun.All on the boat are believed to have been accounted for.The thousands of migrants who cross the Channel are usually brought to shore by border security command or RNLI boats but this one is thought to have slipped through undetected.No small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort have been officially recorded since 6 September, 2025.Kent Police said it became aware of the incident at about 09:25 BST on Monday."Patrols attended and five people were detained and passed to border security command officers," the force said.The Home Office called the incident "isolated and rare". It said: "Officers responded quickly, detaining five individuals. There is an ongoing investigation and it would be inappropriate to comment further."Also on Monday, people in life jackets were pictured being taken into the border security command compound in Dover.Other migrant dinghies were also believed to be in the Channel, with French lifeboat and navy vessels tracking one as far west as Normandy.Some 17,480 migrants have arrived after crossing the Channel by boat so far this year, including 5,011 since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.The 2026 total is down 46% on this time last year.Additional reporting by PA Media.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external,  X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: What we found in Earl Spencer's controversial Diana memoir
description: The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should
body: The coverage has been driven by a simple question: should we believe Earl Spencer's claims about the King's callousness after Diana's death? Or should we believe the unusually robust denial from Buckingham Palace?But when you read further through the book, there's a more complicated story being told.Earl Spencer is the brother watching events unfolding in the strange and ultimately doomed life of his sister, who has stepped from being his childhood companion to become one of the most famous women in the world.He describes a kind of grief and irritation as Diana becomes public property and then royal property, which irks him even more, disliking the "nonsense of fawning" around the monarchy.It's a stark reminder that Diana was only just 20 years old when she married - becoming a global superstar - and was dead 16 years later.Earl Spencer depicts her as a caring, generous character who was haunted by self-doubt, dogged by eating disorders, lacking in warmth from her new royal family and then ultimately dragged down by the tabloid media."She craved acceptance, admiration, kindness, and - perhaps above all - love," writes Charles Spencer about Diana."She got stuck into gritty, controversial, but crucial causes partly because she had a fine, natural social conscience, but also to assuage nagging feelings of worthlessness."And with a memoir like this it will be the extra details that will fascinate people.The stepmother to Diana and Charles, Raine Spencer, is painted in an unflattering light, and Diana is described as getting so angry once that she pushed Raine down the staircase at their home in Althorp. "Raine fortunately landed flush on her buttocks, rather than on bone, and got up, leaving the saloon without a backwards glance," he writes. It was in response, says the book, to Raine telling Diana: "I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you."There's not a single mention of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, even though she was talked about in the TV interviewsWe're told that a "nephew" wanted Earl Spencer to be in a documentary about Diana, which will raise speculation about Prince Harry's plans for his mother's 30th anniversary next yearThe book recounts that she disliked Dodi Fayed's father, Mohammed Fayed, accusing him of crudely groping herDiana's preferences included the soap opera Crossroads and the music of David Bowie. She'd watched The Sound of Music 16 times and the paper she read was the Daily MailEarl Spencer will ultimately be remembered by the passionate eulogy he delivered at Diana's funeral in Westminster Abbey.He reveals how he had pretended to have lost his copy of his speech at the rehearsal, so no one could hear it in advance and try to tone down his stinging criticism of the press and the royals.After the hounding of Diana by the paparazzi, he says he personally rang tabloid newspaper editors to disinvite them from the Abbey funeral, after their invitations had already been sent out.She was buried on an island in the Spencers' Althorp estate, rather than a graveyard - and the book describes how a bishop was brought to consecrate the ground to make it possible.Much of the interest in this book has been driven by its settling of old scores with the Royal Family. It can feel like medieval barons jousting.References to King Charles are almost all negative, including the suggestion that he was jealous of his wife's public popularity.The book reports a conversation in which it's claimed the then-Prince Charles complained: "I mean, I'm 43,' he said, 'and I employ fifty people' – he was flushed in the face now – 'but my parents insist on treating me like – like a child!'"The King is portrayed as resentful, with a "senior courtier" reporting an alleged comment by the late Queen: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet."There's a bizarre account of discussions in the Royal Family about whether the then-Prince Charles's ears should have been pinned back.And there's the allegation that Diana had said the King was in love with his valet, which the author himself says seemed improbable.What comes across is how close the Spencers were to the royals - but without being friends. Charles and Diana Spencer went to the same children's parties as the young royals.The royals are depicted as the type of children who come round, break your toys and then disappear, in what might be an extended metaphor for how he saw Diana's story.There's also a story about a teenage Prince Andrew smirking in a church service because the priest used the word "womb".While the TV interviews have sought Spencer's views on Prince Harry and Prince William, the book doesn't go there.Earl Spencer describes his opposition to the boys having to walk behind the coffin at their mother's funeral - and he talks of "how tiny, and slight, and bereft, Harry looked".But the focus of this book is much more about the Diana era - and an elegy to the lost world of their childhood.Earl Spencer emphasises its country house happiness, with dens, dogs and horses, but it's also dotted with cruelty, with violent nannies and the "mindless and often destructive" tradition of boarding schools.A boy who accidentally shot and killed his father gets the mawkish nickname "Baghdad".Although the book is about Diana, it's also about its author, the younger brother trying to make sense of what's happened - and also, like many younger brothers, being able to criticise without being able to take responsibility.Earl Spencer talks about how little he cares for "archaic" titles for the aristocracy or royals.And in this book, the title that seems really to have shaped his life most is "Diana's brother".Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, by Charles Spencer. Published by Penguin.

schema.headline: What we found in Earl Spencer's controversial Diana memoir

title: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years ByCamilla HorroxHealth report
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years ByCamilla HorroxHealth reporterSocial media is driving the trend for "flawless complexions" and complex "glass skin" routines in teenagers, with many prioritising advice from influencers in Get Ready With Me (GRWM) videos over professionals. But do teens really need a multi-step skincare routine?For consultant dermatologist Dr Jonathan Kentley, the most concerning influence social media is having is the "relentless images of unrealistic beauty standards"."I've seen thousands of patients and I've never seen anyone with 'glass skin'. I don't think it exists, and it's just these over-filtered images that make children think that this is achievable when it's not."Visible pores, blackheads, blemishes, pigmentation, redness and scarring are all very normal for teenage skin, says Dr Kentley. But he adds that everyone's normal is different: "I don't think there's anything that is really abnormal."Figure caption, Is our skin care routine actually making it worse?More than 80% of 13- to 18-year-olds experience acne during their teenage years.Dr Zainab Laftah, a consultant dermatologist, explains that most of the so-called problems you encounter during puberty are related to testosterone, which drives rises in oil production and acne.Boys can experience more of these problems, but girls have testosterone as well so get many of the same symptoms."This, together with blocked hair follicles and inflammation, leads to blackheads, whiteheads and inflamed spots," Dr Laftah says. "Acne is very, very common and it's normal and treatable."Salicylic acid, a common active ingredient that penetrates into oil-filled pores to help clear the buildup of sebum and dead skin cells "can be particularly helpful for teenagers with oily or acne-prone skin" says Dr Laftah, warning that unnecessary or excessive use may cause dryness and irritation.If you're suffering from severe acne or a severe skin problem, Dr Kentley advises getting help from your GP or a dermatologist rather than engaging with people on social media on how to manage it.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Social media is fuelling the trend for "flawless complexions" and multi-step "glass skin" routinesSo, how best to look after teenage skin? Experts Dr Zainab Laftah and Dr Jonathan Kentley share their five top tips:Keep your skincare routine simple You need three basics: a gentle cleanser, a fragrance-free moisturiser and a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher. That's it.More skincare products aren't necessarily better A complicated routine with frequent exfoliations or strong acids can irritate young skin. Remember the skin barrier is still developing and it can result in damage. Dr Kently says he's seen an exponential rise in a condition called perioral dermatitis in teens, which is related to the overuse of ingredients that strip skin barriers like exfoliating hydroxy acids and retinoids. Dr Laftah adds: "Teens are increasingly adopting adult-style routines with numerous serums, toners, masks and actives. These actives are likely to result in skin barrier compromise and lead to more skin issues."Getting enough sleep and a balanced diet is important Raised cortisol through diets high in white carbohydrates and sugar as well as a lack of sleep have been linked to breakouts. Dr Laftah is a supporter of getting a good night's sleep. "We know that a lack of sleep increases cortisol levels, which is a stress hormone that can lead to acne breakouts." While Dr Kentley says a diet that is high in carbohydrate foods, like white rice and pasta, high sugar diets and whey protein found in protein shakes have all been linked in studies to acne flare-ups. But he makes the point that everyone's skin is individual and that "some people may find that other things flare up their skin".Don't pick or pop your spots The risk is that you can increase the inflammation by pushing the content deeper into the skin, which can result in scarring and discolouration. Dr Laftah says she's a fan of the pimple hydrocolloid star patches as a social media hack. "They work by absorbing fluid from superficial spots while creating a protective barrier that discourages picking," she explains.See a GP or dermatologist If you have persistent painful cystic or scarring acne, seek medical advice, as often prescription-grade treatment is needed.What about boys? A lot of the so-called "problems" during teenage years are related to androgens, a hormone which, although present in girls, is more prevalent in boys. "So male skin can sometimes be a little bit more oily and potentially have some more spots, and often you're getting to grips with the concept of facial hair and shaving, and that can introduce irritation," explains Dr Kentley."If you're not shaving properly you can develop quite a lot of folliculitis which is a bit of a crossover from acne. So you can cause quite a lot of damage to the skin barrier, a lot of inflammation."Here are Dr Kentley's top tips for shaving to protect skin:Shave after showering so that the skin is hot, has been steamed and prepared for a shaveUse a shaving brush to lift the hairs off the skinShave with something lubricating like shaving foam or shower gelAlways shave in the direction of travel of the hairs

schema.headline: The simple skincare routine for teens that actually works - and five expert tips

title: Jose Mourinho: Atletico Madrid hit back at Real Madrid boss over referee complaints
description: Mourinho's side had defender Dean Huijsen sent off early in the second half, when the game was goalless, for pulling down Atletico's Giuliano Simeone
body: Mourinho's side had defender Dean Huijsen sent off early in the second half, when the game was goalless, for pulling down Atletico's Giuliano Simeone just inside the penalty area.The match outcome was Real's second defeat of the season, having lost 1-0 to Real Betis earlier in September."We can skip the press conference because the story of the match is right here," Mourinho said as he showed media the printed images on sheets of A4 paper on Sunday."Those were two clear red cards. Given the difficulties we faced afterwards playing 11 against 10, we can only imagine what 50 minutes of 11 against nine would have been like."So I'll just have to limit myself to hugging my players, who gave it their all and played a first half, showed great class and character, setting us up perfectly to win the second half."Simeone, when asked to respond to Mourinho's refereeing rant, said he was always respectful of everyone else's opinions."I understand that we're in a privileged position with a lot of public scrutiny, as coaches, and whether it's Mourinho, [Barcelona manager Hansi] Flick, [Real Betis boss Manuel] Pellegrini, me, or anyone else, we need to be careful about what we say," he said."We have to know how to respect others, the referees, our colleagues. And when someone crosses that line of respect, it's not right - you can't cross that line."

schema.headline: Jose Mourinho: Atletico Madrid hit back at Real Madrid boss over referee complaints

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
description: Trump, reacting to news of the lawsuit, called the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean"
body: Trump, reacting to news of the lawsuit, called the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.He added that "almost without question" his team will file an appeal.The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.The statement from CNN, Politico and MS NOW said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."The media organisations filed the lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington, asking a judge to quickly rule Trump's ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.On Monday morning, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties, which sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday.But on Monday morning, the five-seat CNN booth in the basement of the White House press area - typically manned throughout the day from the early hours of the morning - was empty and closed. Screens and monitors inside were turned off.Instead, a CNN crew was outside the secured area of the White House grounds, broadcasting live from a public pavement.Five TV networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, issued a joint statement: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government."No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."Those five networks are considered the only ones with the money and infrastructure to distribute live coverage from the White House and presidential events.For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.Several US outlets also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday.Later on Monday, Trump met with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for an hour-long discussion. Afterwards, the two held a news conference, which was covered by New York media."I told the president that we're going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in," Mamdani said.Trump continued his criticism of the media at the event, saying that journalists always say that they will boycott, but they "never boycott" him.On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel on its site called Trump TV, which began by replaying remarks from Trump during a visit to Mount Rushmore in July.Announcing his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".The US president added that there "may be others to join them".When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS Now and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban

title: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month
description: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJ
body: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights.EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the service, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.Nats said a "connectivity issue" at Prestwick was behind the disruption across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - and had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick earlier this month.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said further issues today "cause even greater concern" about the UK's air traffic control.When asked by reporters whether he would look to fire the head of Nats, Burnham said "these are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated".He added that the transport secretary was taking the issues "extremely seriously" and initially it's a matter for her "to get to the bottom of... and why there has been a recurrence."The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity", although officials warned of knock-on effects.A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".More than 150 flights were cancelled at UK airports on Monday - including 140 departures and 137 arrivals, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 48 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 13 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".An independent review by the CAA into the resilience of the UK's air traffic control system is under way and the results will be published "within six months", it said.Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure". Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.Asked on BBC Radio 4's World at One programme if Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".A Nats spokesperson apologised, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible."What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation was "deeply frustrating" for passengers. Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot".He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their EasyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning.Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled.She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived.Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time".

schema.headline: Flight disruption: Airlines criticise air traffic control over second glitch in a month

title: Two whales dead in Northumberland after mass stranding
description: The BDMLR said it was not the same pod of whales which was herded out of the River Thames at the weekend as the distance between the locations was fur
body: The BDMLR said it was not the same pod of whales which was herded out of the River Thames at the weekend as the distance between the locations was further than the species could swim in 24 hours.Local boats were launched with medics on board to try to herd the whales offshore to stop them from stranding.But the animals remained tightly packed around one of the largest, which was lying motionless on its side.The teams were stood down after losing the light on Sunday.Earlier on Monday, the BDMLR said about a dozen had been stranded on Coquet Island around rocky terrain.On investigation, six animals were found - five ashore and one afloat.Two of the stranded whales were confirmed to have died, the BDMLR said.Due to the tides and limited access to the island, attempts to refloat the live animals were not possible and the teams withdrew once again.The BDMLR said it would remain along the coast, ready to provide care and attempt to refloat those which were healthy enough.The RSPB said its staff from nearby Coquet Island were continuing to support the BDMLR's response to the incident."This is a distressing situation and our thoughts are with all those involved in the response," a spokesperson said.Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

title: Bishop of Lincoln resigns amid sexual assault inquiry
description: The Bishop of Lincoln, the Right Reverend Stephen Conway, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into an allegation of sexual assault.It follows h
body: The Bishop of Lincoln, the Right Reverend Stephen Conway, has resigned amid an ongoing investigation into an allegation of sexual assault.It follows his arrest in February.Conway's resignation, which will formally come into effect on 1 October, was confirmed in a statement from the Church of England."The complaint process is ongoing. Clergy remain subject to church disciplinary procedures following resignation or retirement," it said.Conway had been suspended from ministry in February when a "safeguarding complaint" was made.At the time, Lincolnshire Police said the arrest was part of an "ongoing investigation following an allegation that a man was sexually assaulted between 2018 and 2025".Following Conway's resignation, the Church said Dr Nicholas Chamberlain, the Bishop of Grantham, would continue as Acting Bishop of Lincoln until a permanent replacement is chosen.Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

title: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
description: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decen
body: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max."We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life". They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5."I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report, external by pension provider Standard Life. And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study, external by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual. Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working. "It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, , externalaccording to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity. The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows., externalBut at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, external.Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays."This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits. The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993)., external However, people can choose to take a lower payment, external from the age of 62.Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.Back in Yorkshire, Sarah is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."

schema.headline: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance

title: 'I want to serve my country but I was rejected on health grounds'
description: 'My army dream was ended by childhood eye surgery'Image caption, Lewis Jackson has been blocked from joining the British Army on medical groundsByNath
body: 'My army dream was ended by childhood eye surgery'Image caption, Lewis Jackson has been blocked from joining the British Army on medical groundsByNathan HeathBBC West InvestigationsLewis Jackson cannot remember a time when he did not want to join the army and continue a family tradition of military service going back to World War One. That dream was shattered, though, when his application was rejected on medical grounds."Serving my country has always been a dream of mine and I never considered that I'd do anything else," said the 21-year-old.Jackson, from Cirencester, was turned down by the Army because he had cataract surgery at the age of three.A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said: "Service in the Armed Forces is physically demanding, so it's right that we have sensible health and recruitment policies which maintain operational effectiveness but don't unnecessarily exclude people."The BBC has spoken to potential recruits and professionals who question whether the rules are too strict while some applicants said they had been prevented from joining because of medical conditions they regard as minor or no longer relevant.Image caption, Jackson spent his teens in the cadets, preparing himself for a career in the ArmyJackson spent his teenage years in the Army Cadets where he was recognised in his unit as the best shot.He applied to join the Army Reserve, motivated by a desire to "give back" to a country which he said had given him "so much", but he was rejected."It's very frustrating, especially when you know that you are fit and healthy and you haven't even been given the opportunity to fail," he said.There were 108,020 applications to the British Army Regular Forces in the year leading up to September 2025.Separate figures obtained under a Freedom of Information (FOI) request to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) showed more than 114,000 applications to the Army were rejected on medical grounds in the past five years.Psychiatry, eye and musculoskeletal conditions were some of the most common reasons for rejection.An MOD spokesperson said: "The majority of these figures cover years before the substantial changes the government has made to remove over 100 outdated and unnecessary recruitment policies."Image source, Lewis JacksonImage caption, Jackson was the top shot in his cadet forceThe figures come against a backdrop of wider recruitment challenges for the armed forces.Latest UK defence personnel report figures showed the military remained at about six percent below its full-time trained strength target with a shortfall of 8,460 personnel.Jackson said he had appealed against the rejection, providing a range of supporting evidence, including a note from a consultant ophthalmic surgeon who said his vision was now "excellent in both eyes" and "everything was stable".But although his vision now meets the standard, he is ineligible because medical entry rules mean applicants who have had lens replacement surgery are considered "unfit" as they need "the visual function to be able to perform their role safely and effectively".He has been told he is "permanently medically unfit to serve".Jackson said: "We are missing out on young men and women who are passionate about serving but instead are pursuing different careers."I think it is ludicrous. If you're fit, you should be able to join."Image source, Lewis JacksonImage caption, One of Jackson's relatives was awarded a medal for bravery during World War OneGP and Labour MP for Stroud Dr Simon Opher said there needed to be a "more sensible approach" to medical screening."If a health condition is stable and it's not affecting someone's functional ability, then there's no reason to exclude that person," he said."We have to get that balance right between what's happened in the past and what would actually affect an armed forces personnel in their day-to-day duties."The MoD sets out the medical standards in a document known as the Joint Service Publication (JSP) 950 Medical Policy.In 2024, it reviewed recruitment policies, including removing a ban on applicants with asthma and severe acne.But for 20-year-old Ben Smith those changes have made little difference as his application was rejected because of ongoing use of an inhaler.Image caption, Ben Smith wanted to follow in the footsteps of his fatherSmith, from Blandford Forum, Dorset, wanted to join the Royal Air Force (RAF) but asthma has prevented him from doing so."There is nothing more I wanted to do in the world," he said."I'd led 250 cadets on parades and then, for all of that to come crashing down when I didn't have a back-up plan, it was horrible."After rising through the cadet ranks, Smith studied military protective services at college and dedicated himself to reaching the fitness standards required for service."I was proud," he said."I was lifting double my body weight in the gym and my bleep test scores were constantly improving."Image source, Ben SmithImage caption, Smith uses an inhaler to treat asthma but he said it did not affect his fitnessInspired by other family members who had served in the armed forces, he applied to join the RAF, hoping to train as either aircrew or a mechanic.However, his application was rejected because he uses an inhaler.Smith's appeal included a letter from his GP which said he had an "unlimited exercise tolerance".The letter said: "He is a fit and active young man with a strong ambition to join."His appeal was unsuccessful.The review said: "All candidates, irrespective of role, need to be a minimum of 12 months treatment, symptom and medication-free."For Smith, the decision brought his life-long ambition to an end."The dream has ended," he said."I've been told no. I don't know what to do with myself."Image source, Stuart CrawfordImage caption, Lt Col Stuart Crawford said the military must "relax its medical policies"Prof Neil Greenberg, president of the Society of Occupational Medicine, said: "The military has to have strict standards of physical and psychological health."It requires people to go all around the globe, often at short notice, and to put up with environments that really are quite unpleasant."It is vital that soldiers can perform to a very high level because if it goes wrong, it could mean loss of life."'Fight my case'Former British Army Lt Col Stuart Crawford, who was previously a defence spokesman for the Scottish National Party (SNP), said the military was "losing out on talent".He said: "Recruitment policies must be in place, of course, but we need to be careful that we are not turning away talent because of minor medical issues."He said this was "increasingly dangerous" in a time of global instability."We're always being told that we could be at war and we are nowhere near rising to that challenge in terms of our recruitment," Crawford said.An MoD spokesperson said: "Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis by specialist clinicians, assessing the severity of any condition and the individual's ability to train, deploy and operate."Jackson said the MoD needed to go "much further" in its review of recruitment policies."We're blanketing out thousands of young men and women," he said.Jackson is currently studying agricultural management at the Royal Agricultural University in Cirencester."I'm in a lucky situation being at university where I have the time to fight my case alongside my studies," he said."But for many people, it's just not feasible to spend hours a week trying to fight the system."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire
